library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
library(here)
library(scales)
library(sf)

rgn_labels <- c(
  "Region_1" = "Western Upper Gulf",
  "Region_2" = "Western Midriff Islands",
  "Region_3" = "Western Central Gulf",
  "Region_4" = "Western Southern Gulf",
  "Region_5" = "Eastern Upper Gulf",
  "Region_6" = "Eastern Midriff Islands",
  "Region_7" = "Southern Sonora Coast",
  "Region_8" = "Sinaloa Coast",
  "Region_9" = "Southeastern Gulf"
)

rgn_colors <- c(
  "Region_1" = "#C03729",
  "Region_2" = "#E68C7C",
  "Region_3" = "#FC8F24",
  "Region_4" = "#dcaa38",
  "Region_5" = "#cbd2a0",
  "Region_6" = "#98a25a",
  "Region_7" = "#747428",
  "Region_8" = "#627391",
  "Region_9" = "#8d61a9"
)

region_levels <- paste0("Region_", 1:9)
rgn_label_colors <- setNames(unname(rgn_colors[region_levels]), unname(rgn_labels[region_levels]))

add_rgn_labels <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      rgn_id = factor(as.character(rgn_id), levels = region_levels),
      rgn_label = factor(
        rgn_labels[as.character(rgn_id)],
        levels = unname(rgn_labels[region_levels])
      )
    )
}

gg_theme_pdf <- function() {
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      legend.position = "right",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
    )
}

cw_plotly_lines <- function(df, y_var, title, y_range = c(0, 105),
                            connect_gaps = TRUE) {
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
    arrange(rgn_label, year)

  y_col <- rlang::sym(y_var)
  year_breaks <- sort(unique(df$year[!is.na(df$year)]))
  # Drop NA years from drawn geometry so the line bridges gaps (e.g. pathogens 2019–2021)
  df_drawn <- if (isTRUE(connect_gaps)) {
    df %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(!!y_col))
  } else {
    df
  }

  p <- ggplot(df_drawn, aes(x = year, y = !!y_col, color = rgn_label, group = rgn_label)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_color_manual(values = rgn_label_colors, name = "Region") +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = year_breaks,
      labels = as.integer(year_breaks),
      limits = range(year_breaks)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Año // Year",
      y = "Puntaje // Percent (out of 100)"
    ) +
    gg_theme_pdf()

  if (!is.null(y_range)) {
    p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = y_range)
  }

  p
}

cw_plotly_goc <- function(df, y_var, title, y_range = c(0, 105),
                          connect_gaps = TRUE) {
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
    arrange(year)

  y_col <- rlang::sym(y_var)
  year_breaks <- sort(unique(df$year[!is.na(df$year)]))
  df_drawn <- if (isTRUE(connect_gaps)) {
    df %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(!!y_col))
  } else {
    df
  }

  p <- ggplot(df_drawn, aes(x = year, y = !!y_col)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#333333") +
    geom_point(size = 2, color = "#333333") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = year_breaks,
      labels = as.integer(year_breaks),
      limits = range(year_breaks)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Año // Year",
      y = "Puntaje // Percent (out of 100)"
    ) +
    gg_theme_pdf() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  if (!is.null(y_range)) {
    p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = y_range)
  }

  p
}

# Prefer Mazu paths; fall back to a local cw_mazu copy when available
pick_existing <- function(...) {
  paths <- unlist(list(...), use.names = FALSE)
  hit <- paths[file.exists(paths)]
  if (length(hit) == 0) NA_character_ else hit[[1]]
}

gg_theme_map <- function() {
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.direction = "horizontal",
      legend.justification = "center",
      legend.box = "vertical",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 7.5),
      legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"),
      legend.key.width = unit(0.7, "cm"),
      # Extra side/bottom margin so Word does not clip the legend
      legend.margin = margin(4, 10, 4, 10),
      legend.box.margin = margin(6, 10, 8, 10),
      plot.margin = margin(10, 18, 18, 18)
    )
}

# TR / Access / LSP-style ramp: 0 = dark red, 100 = blue
cw_score_palette <- c(
  "#8a0032", "#A50026", "#A50026", "#D73027", "#F46D43",
  "#FDAE61", "#FEE090", "#FEE090", "#ABD9E9", "#4575B4", "#313695"
)
cw_na_fill <- "white"

normalize_rgn_id <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    as.character() %>%
    stringr::str_squish() %>%
    stringr::str_replace_all(" ", "_")
}

cw_map_choropleth <- function(regions_sf, scores_df, title, subtitle = NULL,
                              states_sf = NULL, label_scores = FALSE) {
  if (is.null(regions_sf) || is.null(scores_df) || nrow(scores_df) == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = paste(title, "(map data unavailable)")))
  }

  latest <- scores_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(final_score)) %>%
    mutate(rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id)) %>%
    group_by(rgn_id) %>%
    filter(year == max(year, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, score = final_score) %>%
    mutate(score = ifelse(is.nan(score), NA_real_, score))

  yr <- unique(latest$year)
  if (is.null(subtitle) && length(yr) > 0) {
    subtitle <- paste0("Snapshot year: ", paste(yr, collapse = ", "))
  }

  dat <- regions_sf %>%
    mutate(rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id)) %>%
    left_join(latest, by = "rgn_id") %>%
    mutate(rgn_label = unname(rgn_labels[rgn_id]))

  p <- ggplot()

  if (!is.null(states_sf)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_sf(
        data = states_sf,
        fill = "#d6cac0",
        color = "grey10",
        linewidth = 0.1
      )
  }

  p <- p +
    geom_sf(
      data = dat,
      aes(fill = score),
      color = "black",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ) +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
      colours = cw_score_palette,
      limits = c(0, 100),
      na.value = cw_na_fill,
      name = "Score",
      breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 25)
    ) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle) +
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
    gg_theme_map()

  if (isTRUE(label_scores)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_sf_text(
        data = dat %>%
          mutate(label = ifelse(is.na(score), "NA", as.character(round(score)))),
        aes(label = label),
        size = 2.8,
        color = "grey10",
        fun.geometry = function(g) sf::st_point_on_surface(sf::st_make_valid(g))
      )
  }

  p
}

# Inland-only ring: marine+10km buffer minus marine polygons (light grey wash)
inland_buffer_ring <- function(buffer_sf, marine_sf) {
  if (is.null(buffer_sf) || is.null(marine_sf)) return(NULL)
  tryCatch({
    buf <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(buffer_sf)))
    mar <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(marine_sf)))
    inland <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_difference(buf, mar))
    if (length(inland) == 0 || all(sf::st_is_empty(inland))) return(NULL)
    sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(id = 1L), geometry = inland)
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
}

cw_map_points_on_regions <- function(regions_sf, points_sf, title, subtitle = NULL,
                                     size = 2.1, states_sf = NULL,
                                     buffer_sf = NULL, inland_sf = NULL) {
  if (is.null(regions_sf) || is.null(points_sf)) {
    return(ggplot() + theme_void() + labs(title = paste(title, "(map data unavailable)")))
  }

  # Colored marine regions; inland 10 km is a separate light-grey wash
  regs <- regions_sf %>%
    mutate(rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id)) %>%
    add_rgn_labels()

  if (is.null(inland_sf) && !is.null(buffer_sf)) {
    inland_sf <- inland_buffer_ring(buffer_sf, regions_sf)
  }

  pts <- points_sf %>%
    mutate(rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id)) %>%
    mutate(
      rgn_label = factor(
        rgn_labels[as.character(rgn_id)],
        levels = unname(rgn_labels[region_levels])
      )
    )

  p <- ggplot()
  if (!is.null(states_sf)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_sf(data = states_sf, fill = "#d6cac0", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.12)
  }

  # See-through inland 10 km buffer only (no heavy outline)
  if (!is.null(inland_sf) && nrow(inland_sf) > 0) {
    p <- p +
      geom_sf(
        data = inland_sf,
        fill = "grey65",
        alpha = 0.22,
        color = NA,
        linewidth = 0
      )
  }

  # Marine regions: soft grey borders so black-outlined points stay readable
  p <- p +
    geom_sf(
      data = regs,
      aes(fill = rgn_label),
      alpha = 0.4,
      color = "grey55",
      linewidth = 0.25,
      show.legend = FALSE
    )

  # Points: larger + thicker black outline for contrast
  p +
    geom_sf(
      data = pts,
      aes(fill = rgn_label),
      shape = 21,
      color = "black",
      stroke = 0.6,
      size = size,
      alpha = 0.95
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = rgn_label_colors, name = "Region") +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle) +
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE, clip = "off") +
    gg_theme_map() +
    guides(
      fill = guide_legend(
        ncol = 2,
        byrow = TRUE,
        title.position = "top",
        override.aes = list(shape = 21, color = "black", stroke = 0.55, size = 2.8, alpha = 1)
      )
    )
}

# Status tables live on Mazu under goal_prep/cw
cw_root <- "/home/shares/ohi/OHI_GOC/goal_prep/cw/v2025"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Eutrophication (EUT): UPDATED METHOD
# Watershed -> pourpoint -> OHI region total nitrogen (JARG update), scored with
# the ALT rescaling (top-5 mean TN per km of coast -> pressure 0.5; status 50-100).
# This replaces the earlier single-snapshot municipal estimate
# (eutrophication/output/eutrophication_cs.csv).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
eut_alt_path <- file.path(
  cw_root,
  "eutrophication/jarg_analysis_update/output/nutrient_status_ALT.csv"
)
if (!file.exists(eut_alt_path)) {
  stop("Updated eutrophication scores (nutrient_status_ALT.csv) not found at: ", eut_alt_path)
}

# Observed multi-year EUT series (no extrapolation) used for the EUT figures
eutro_obs <- read_csv(eut_alt_path, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score = status) %>%
  filter(year %in% 2017:2025)

# Series completed to the common 2017-2025 CW window (carry nearest observed value),
# used only when overall CW must be rebuilt from its components
eutro_cs <- eutro_obs %>%
  group_by(rgn_id) %>%
  complete(year = 2017:2025) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  fill(final_score, .direction = "downup") %>%
  ungroup()

# Updated pathogens series (2018-2025; 2020 left missing for the COVID pause)
path_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "pathogens/output/pathogen_cs_2018_2025.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score = current_status) %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    final_score = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(final_score))
  ) %>%
  group_by(rgn_id) %>%
  tidyr::complete(year = 2018:2025) %>%
  # Explicit COVID pause: keep the year on the axis, but no score / no point
  mutate(final_score = ifelse(year == 2020, NA_real_, final_score)) %>%
  ungroup()

chem_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "chemicals/chemical_cs.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score = chemical_cs,
                PEST, PHRM, WWPS, HAZW, VESS) %>%
  group_by(rgn_id) %>%
  complete(year = 2017:2025) %>%
  fill(final_score, PEST, PHRM, WWPS, HAZW, VESS, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup()

pest_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "chemicals/pesticides/output/cw_chemical_pesticide_current_status.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score = current_status_final)

phrm_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "chemicals/pharmaceuticals/current_status_pharmaceuticals.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score = current_status_final)

hazw_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "chemicals/hazardous_waste/output/current_status_hazardous_waste.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year = anio, final_score)

wwps_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "chemicals/agua_sin_tratamiento/output/untreated_ww_current_status.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year = census_year, final_score = current_status_final)

vess_cs <- chem_cs %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score = VESS) %>%
  filter(!is.na(final_score))

pla_cs <- read_csv(
  file.path(cw_root, "marine_debris/ghost_gear_risk.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(final_score = (1 - pressure) * 100) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score)

# Component table (EUT, PAT, CHM, MAR) used for reporting and as the rebuild fallback
cw_components <- eutro_cs %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
  dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, EUT = final_score) %>%
  full_join(
    path_cs %>% mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>% dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, PAT = final_score),
    by = c("rgn_id", "year")
  ) %>%
  full_join(
    chem_cs %>% mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>% dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, CHM = final_score),
    by = c("rgn_id", "year")
  ) %>%
  full_join(
    pla_cs %>% mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>% dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, MAR = final_score),
    by = c("rgn_id", "year")
  ) %>%
  filter(year %in% 2017:2025)

# Overall CW = arithmetic mean of EUT, PAT, CHM, MAR (updated EUT)
cw_rebuild <- function() {
  cw_components %>%
    mutate(
      final_score = rowMeans(cbind(EUT, PAT, CHM, MAR), na.rm = TRUE),
      final_score = ifelse(is.nan(final_score), NA_real_, final_score)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score)
}

cw_updated_path <- file.path(cw_root, "cw_current_status_arithmetic_w_updated_EUTR.csv")
cw_status <- NULL
cw_source_note <- "rebuilt"

if (file.exists(cw_updated_path)) {
  cw_status_raw <- read_csv(cw_updated_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  cw_score_col <- intersect(c("CW", "final_score", "current_status", "cw"), names(cw_status_raw))[1]
  if (!is.na(cw_score_col)) {
    cw_status <- cw_status_raw %>%
      mutate(year = as.numeric(year), final_score = .data[[cw_score_col]]) %>%
      dplyr::select(rgn_id, year, final_score) %>%
      filter(year %in% 2017:2025)
    cw_source_note <- "precomputed"
  }
}
if (is.null(cw_status)) {
  cw_status <- cw_rebuild()

safe_read_sf <- function(path) {
  if (is.na(path) || !file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  tryCatch(sf::st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
}

prep_rgn_polygons <- function(x, marine_only = FALSE) {
  if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)
  if (!"rgn_id" %in% names(x)) {
    id_alt <- intersect(c("rgn", "region_id", "REGION_ID", "id"), names(x))
    if (length(id_alt) > 0) {
      names(x)[names(x) == id_alt[[1]]] <- "rgn_id"
    }
  }
  if (!"rgn_id" %in% names(x)) return(NULL)
  if (isTRUE(marine_only) && "location" %in% names(x)) {
    x <- x %>% dplyr::filter(tolower(as.character(location)) == "marine")
  }
  x %>%
    mutate(rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id)) %>%
    group_by(rgn_id) %>%
    summarise(.groups = "drop")
}

# Align CRS to regions when possible
align_to_regions <- function(x) {

# Assign every point to an OHI region without dropping any features.
# Prefer marine+inland buffer polygons; fall back to nearest region if no overlap.
assign_points_to_regions <- function(pts, poly_sf, label = "points") {
  if (is.null(pts) || nrow(pts) == 0) return(pts)
  n0 <- nrow(pts)

  if (is.null(poly_sf) || nrow(poly_sf) == 0) {
    message(label, ": no region polygons for assignment; keeping ", n0, " points")
    return(pts)
  }

  pts <- tryCatch(sf::st_make_valid(pts), error = function(e) pts)
  poly <- poly_sf %>%
    mutate(rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id)) %>%
    dplyr::select(rgn_id)

  hits <- tryCatch(
    sf::st_intersects(pts, poly),
    error = function(e) vector("list", n0)
  )
  rgn_vec <- vapply(seq_len(n0), function(i) {
    ix <- hits[[i]]
    if (is.null(ix) || length(ix) == 0) {
      NA_character_
    } else {
      as.character(poly$rgn_id[[ix[[1]]]])
    }
  }, character(1))

  miss <- which(is.na(rgn_vec) | rgn_vec == "")
  if (length(miss) > 0) {
    near_ix <- tryCatch(
      sf::st_nearest_feature(pts[miss, ], poly),
      error = function(e) integer(0)
    )
    if (length(near_ix) == length(miss)) {
      rgn_vec[miss] <- as.character(poly$rgn_id[near_ix])
      message(label, ": assigned ", length(miss), " points by nearest region (no overlap)")
    }
  }

  pts$rgn_id <- normalize_rgn_id(rgn_vec)
  tab <- sort(table(as.character(pts$rgn_id), useNA = "ifany"), decreasing = TRUE)
  message(
    label, ": kept ", nrow(pts), " of ", n0, " points. By region: ",
    paste(names(tab), tab, sep = "=", collapse = ", ")
  )
  pts
}

# GoC-side pourpoint filter (same idea as pesticide prep on Mazu):
# 1) keep points inside marine + 50 km inland (needed for Region_5 / Colorado delta)
# 2) for western Baja dual-coast regions, also require marine + 10 km so Pacific
#    outlets are dropped. BCS is Region_4; Regions 1–3 have the same Pacific-backside issue.
filter_pourpoints_goc_side <- function(
    pts,
    buffer50,
    buffer10,
    tight_10km_regions = c("Region_1", "Region_2", "Region_3", "Region_4")
) {
  if (is.null(pts) || nrow(pts) == 0) return(pts)
  n0 <- nrow(pts)

  if (is.null(buffer50) || nrow(buffer50) == 0) {
    message("GoC pourpoint filter: no 50 km buffer available; leaving ", n0, " points unchanged")
    return(pts)
  }

  pts <- tryCatch(sf::st_make_valid(pts), error = function(e) pts)
  buf50 <- tryCatch(sf::st_make_valid(buffer50), error = function(e) buffer50)

  pts50 <- tryCatch(
    sf::st_filter(pts, buf50),
    error = function(e) {
      tryCatch(
        suppressWarnings(sf::st_intersection(pts, sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(buf50)))),
        error = function(e2) pts
      )
    }
  )
  if (is.null(pts50) || nrow(pts50) == 0) {
    message("GoC pourpoint filter: none of ", n0, " points fall in the 50 km buffer")
    return(pts50)
  }

  pts50 <- assign_points_to_regions(pts50, buf50, label = "GoC 50 km pour points")

  if (!is.null(buffer10) && nrow(buffer10) > 0) {
    buf10 <- tryCatch(sf::st_make_valid(buffer10), error = function(e) buffer10)
    in10 <- tryCatch(
      lengths(sf::st_intersects(pts50, sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(buf10)))) > 0,
      error = function(e) rep(TRUE, nrow(pts50))
    )
    rgn_chr <- normalize_rgn_id(pts50$rgn_id)
    drop_pacific <- rgn_chr %in% tight_10km_regions & !in10
    message(
      "GoC pourpoint filter: dropped ", sum(drop_pacific, na.rm = TRUE),
      " western-Baja Pacific-side points outside 10 km (",
      paste(tight_10km_regions, collapse = ", "),
      "); kept ", sum(!drop_pacific, na.rm = TRUE), " of ", n0
    )
    pts50 <- pts50[!drop_pacific, ]
  } else {
    message(
      "GoC pourpoint filter: kept ", nrow(pts50),
      " of ", n0, " points inside 50 km (no 10 km layer for Baja trim)"
    )
  }

  pts50
}

  } else {
    regs <- regions_sf %>% add_rgn_labels()
    p <- ggplot()

    # Full GoC watershed polygons first (these extend inland across surrounding states)
    ws_plot <- NULL
    if (!is.null(watersheds_sf) && nrow(watersheds_sf) > 0) {
      ws_plot <- tryCatch(st_make_valid(watersheds_sf), error = function(e) watersheds_sf)
      p <- p +
        geom_sf(
          data = ws_plot,
          fill = "#d9d2c5",
          alpha = 0.55,
          color = "grey35",
          linewidth = 0.22
        )
    }

    # Optional states underlay on top of watersheds only as outlines (if available)
    if (!is.null(states_sf)) {
      p <- p +
        geom_sf(
          data = states_sf,
          fill = NA,
          color = "grey20",
          linewidth = 0.35
        )
    }

    if (!is.null(inland10_sf) && nrow(inland10_sf) > 0) {
      p <- p +
        geom_sf(
          data = inland10_sf,
          fill = "grey65",
          alpha = 0.18,
          color = NA,
          linewidth = 0
        )
    }

    p <- p +
      geom_sf(
        data = regs,
        aes(fill = rgn_label),
        alpha = 0.45,
        color = "grey55",
        linewidth = 0.25
      )

    # Pour points already GoC-filtered (50 km, with western Baja tightened to 10 km)
    point_fill_scale <- rgn_label_colors
    pts <- if (!is.null(pourpoints_base_sf)) pourpoints_base_sf else pest_pp_sf
    if (!is.null(pts)) {
      if (!"rgn_id" %in% names(pts) || all(is.na(pts$rgn_id))) {
        assign_poly <- if (!is.null(rgn_buffer50_sf)) rgn_buffer50_sf else rgn_buffer_sf
        pts <- assign_points_to_regions(pts, assign_poly, label = "overview pour points")
      }
      pts <- pts %>%
        mutate(
          rgn_id = normalize_rgn_id(rgn_id),
          rgn_label = factor(
            dplyr::coalesce(
              unname(rgn_labels[as.character(rgn_id)]),
              "Unassigned"
            ),
            levels = c(unname(rgn_labels[region_levels]), "Unassigned")
          )
        )
      message(
        "Overview map pour points: ", nrow(pts),
        " | Region_1: ", sum(as.character(pts$rgn_id) == "Region_1", na.rm = TRUE)
      )

      point_fill_scale <- c(rgn_label_colors, "Unassigned" = "white")
      p <- p +
        geom_sf(
          data = pts,
          aes(fill = rgn_label),
          shape = 21,
          color = "black",
          stroke = 0.45,
          size = 1.6,
          alpha = 0.95,
          show.legend = FALSE
        )
    }

    # Expand view to include full watershed extent, not only marine polygons
    map_xlim <- NULL
    map_ylim <- NULL
    if (!is.null(ws_plot) && nrow(ws_plot) > 0) {
      bb <- tryCatch({
        bb_ws <- sf::st_bbox(ws_plot)
        bb_rg <- sf::st_bbox(regs)
        c(
          xmin = min(bb_ws["xmin"], bb_rg["xmin"], na.rm = TRUE),
          xmax = max(bb_ws["xmax"], bb_rg["xmax"], na.rm = TRUE),
          ymin = min(bb_ws["ymin"], bb_rg["ymin"], na.rm = TRUE),
          ymax = max(bb_ws["ymax"], bb_rg["ymax"], na.rm = TRUE)
        )
      }, error = function(e) NULL)
      if (!is.null(bb) && all(is.finite(bb))) {
        pad_x <- 0.15 * (bb["xmax"] - bb["xmin"])
        pad_y <- 0.08 * (bb["ymax"] - bb["ymin"])
        map_xlim <- c(bb["xmin"] - pad_x, bb["xmax"] + pad_x)
        map_ylim <- c(bb["ymin"] - pad_y, bb["ymax"] + pad_y)
      }
    }

    p +
      scale_fill_manual(
        values = point_fill_scale,
        name = "Region",
        breaks = unname(rgn_labels[region_levels]),
        na.value = "white"
      ) +
      labs(
        title = "GoC watersheds, pour points, and OHI regions",
        subtitle = "Tan = watersheds; colored = marine OHI regions; pour points = GoC-side only (50 km; western Baja 10 km)"
      ) +
      {
        if (!is.null(map_xlim) && !is.null(map_ylim)) {
          coord_sf(xlim = map_xlim, ylim = map_ylim, expand = FALSE, clip = "off")
        } else {
          coord_sf(expand = FALSE, clip = "off")
        }
      } +
      gg_theme_map() +
      guides(
        fill = guide_legend(
          ncol = 2,
          byrow = TRUE,
          title.position = "top"
        )
      )
  }
}

# Summary statistics used for in-text reporting (latest available year per component)
fmt1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)

summ_cs <- function(df) {
  d <- df %>%
    mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
    filter(!is.na(final_score))
  g <- d %>%
    group_by(year) %>%
    summarize(m = mean(final_score, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(year)
  yr <- max(d$year)
  dl <- d %>%
    filter(year == yr) %>%
    add_rgn_labels() %>%
    arrange(desc(final_score))
  list(
    yr = yr,
    first_yr = g$year[1],
    first = g$m[1],
    last = g$m[nrow(g)],
    hi_lab = as.character(dl$rgn_label[1]),
    hi = dl$final_score[1],
    lo_lab = as.character(dl$rgn_label[nrow(dl)]),
    lo = dl$final_score[nrow(dl)]
  )
}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Clean coastal waters are valued for human health, recreation, seafood safety, and aesthetic reasons, yet the pollutants that degrade them reach the sea through multiple pathways. We applied a regional Ocean Health Index (OHI) framework to score the Clean Waters (CW) goal across nine marine regions of the Gulf of California. The CW goal is the arithmetic mean of four components: Eutrophication (EUT), Pathogens (PAT), Chemicals (CHM), and Marine Debris (MAR). Chemicals is the arithmetic mean of five subcomponents: pesticides, pharmaceuticals, hazardous waste sites, untreated wastewater discharge points, and vessel hydrocarbons. A score of 100 represents the reference condition for each indicator. A key update in this assessment is the replacement of the earlier single-snapshot, municipality-based eutrophication estimate with a multi-year, watershed-based total nitrogen (TN) model that sums wastewater, agricultural, livestock, and shrimp aquaculture sources, routes them through watershed pour points to OHI regions, standardizes them by coastline length, and scores them against the mean of the five highest TN loads per kilometer of coast, with pressure rescaled so that eutrophication status ranges from 50 to 100. Under the updated method, the Gulf-wide mean CW score in `r s_cw$yr` was approximately `r fmt1(s_cw$last)` out of 100, with regional scores ranging from `r fmt1(s_cw$lo)` (`r s_cw$lo_lab`) to `r fmt1(s_cw$hi)` (`r s_cw$hi_lab`). Component and subcomponent results show that the pathways driving contamination differ among regions. Plastic pollution and microplastics were explored but are not scored because standardized, repeated, region-level monitoring data are not available. The assessment illustrates how a goal-driven OHI framing can integrate disparate land-based and marine datasets into a transparent, repeatable regional scorecard of clean waters.

# Introduction

As decision-makers shift toward more comprehensive approaches to managing coastal and marine ecosystems, management goals increasingly focus on overall ocean health rather than single sectors or stressors. The Ocean Health Index (OHI) was developed to measure how well marine systems sustainably deliver a portfolio of benefits that people need and desire, including food provision, livelihoods, tourism and recreation, biodiversity, and clean waters (Halpern et al. 2012). Regional applications of the Index adapt goal models and reference points to locally available data and policy priorities while retaining a comparable 0–100 scoring structure (Halpern et al. 2014).

The Clean Waters (CW) goal measures the degree to which local waters are unpolluted by anthropogenic sources. People value marine waters that are free of pollution and debris for aesthetic and health reasons, are especially sensitive to contamination in areas they use for recreation, and place a high existence value on simply knowing that clean waters exist. Contamination reaches coastal waters through several pathways, including nutrient loading that can lead to eutrophication, disease-causing pathogens from sewage, agricultural and industrial chemicals, pharmaceuticals, hydrocarbons from vessels, and floating or abandoned debris. For most of these pressures the status score is the inverse of intensity: high contamination yields a low status score, and the goal scores highest when contamination is near zero. The CW goal is therefore distinct from the economic cost of pollution or the jobs and revenue generated by marine industries, which are treated under Livelihoods and Economies in the OHI framework.

The Gulf of California is a semi-enclosed sea bordered by arid watersheds and by several of the most productive agricultural, aquaculture, and livestock-producing regions of Mexico. Land-based activity in these watersheds, together with the wastewater of coastal cities and the intensity of regional fishing, creates multiple potential contamination pathways, and the relative importance of each pathway varies along the Gulf. Evaluating clean waters in this setting requires indicators that connect inland activity to the coastal region where its effects are most likely to be experienced, together with indicators that are based on direct measurements where these are available.

Here we present a regional CW assessment for the Gulf of California OHI. We address four questions: (1) How can eutrophication, pathogens, chemicals, and marine debris be operationalized with Mexican national and regional datasets? (2) How do CW scores vary across nine OHI regions and over time? (3) How does an updated, multi-year, watershed-based nitrogen method for eutrophication change the representation of nutrient pressure relative to the earlier single-snapshot municipal estimate? (4) Which data gaps and reference-point decisions remain for future refinement? We structure the paper as an Introduction–Methods–Results–Discussion narrative, while retaining the full set of component and subcomponent figures used in the technical assessment.

# Methods

## Study region and spatial framework

CW current-status scores were calculated for nine OHI marine regions of the Gulf of California (Western and Eastern Upper Gulf, Western and Eastern Midriff Islands, Western Central Gulf, Western Southern Gulf, Southern Sonora Coast, Sinaloa Coast, and Southeastern Gulf), plus a simple Gulf-wide mean of regional scores. Scores are reported for the years for which each component is available (Eutrophication: `r eut_years_txt`; Pathogens: 2018–2025; Chemicals and Marine Debris: through 2025). A score of 100 denotes the indicator-specific reference condition.

Many CW pressures originate on land. For these, the general approach was to estimate how much pressure originates in each watershed, to assign that pressure to the OHI region where the watershed drains to the coast through its pour point, and to convert higher pressure into a lower status score. Pour points were restricted to those on the Gulf side of the peninsula, using a 50 km inland buffer around the marine regions (needed to capture, for example, the Colorado River delta) and a tighter 10 km inland buffer for the western Baja California regions so that Pacific-draining outlets were excluded (Figure 1). For several indicators the reference condition representing the lowest score was based on the mean of the five highest pressure values observed across regions and years, so that a single extreme observation did not define the entire scale. The resulting scores are therefore relative rankings within the Gulf of California assessment and should not be interpreted as legal compliance determinations. Pathogens are the exception because Mexican regulation provides an explicit beach suitability threshold.

## Goal model

Following the OHI philosophy that people are part of the social–ecological system, CW measures how free coastal waters are from pollution caused by people, with an emphasis on multiple contamination pathways. The overall score for region $r$ and year $t$ is the arithmetic mean of four components:

$$
\text{CW}_{r,t} = \frac{\text{EUT}_{r,t} + \text{PAT}_{r,t} + \text{CHM}_{r,t} + \text{MAR}_{r,t}}{4}
$$

Chemicals is in turn the arithmetic mean of five subcomponents with equal weights:

$$
\text{CHM}_{r,t} = \frac{\text{PEST}_{r,t} + \text{PHRM}_{r,t} + \text{HAZW}_{r,t} + \text{WWPS}_{r,t} + \text{VESS}_{r,t}}{5}
$$

where PEST is pesticides, PHRM is pharmaceuticals, HAZW is hazardous waste sites, WWPS is untreated wastewater discharge points, and VESS is vessel hydrocarbons. Where a component is not available for a given region and year (for example, Pathogens in 2020), the overall score is the mean of the available components.

A geometric mean was considered for the overall goal so that one poorly performing pathway could not be averaged away. In practice, the geometric mean produced implausibly low CW scores where a single pathway reached the ceiling of its reference point as a scaling artifact, most notably ghost gear risk in the Sinaloa Coast (Region 8) in 2017. An arithmetic mean was therefore adopted because it was considered more representative of overall clean-waters condition across the four pathways, and it remains sensitive to every component without allowing a reference-point artifact to remove the contribution of the others.

| Component | What it measures |
|-----------|------------------|
| Eutrophication (EUT) | Excess nitrogen reaching the coast from wastewater, agriculture, livestock, and shrimp aquaculture, estimated by watershed and assigned to regions through pour points |
| Pathogens (PAT) | Enterococcus levels at monitored beaches (*Playas Limpias* program) |
| Chemicals (CHM) | Mean of pesticides, pharmaceuticals, hazardous waste sites, untreated wastewater discharge points, and vessel hydrocarbon risk |
| Marine Debris (MAR) | Risk of abandoned, lost, and discarded fishing gear (ghost gear); plastic pollution and microplastics explored but not scored |

## Eutrophication (EUT): updated watershed-based nitrogen method

*Motivation and the earlier method.* Chlorophyll *a* (chl-a) was initially explored as an indicator of eutrophication risk by comparing annual mean concentrations in nearshore (5, 10, and 15 km) and offshore zones for each region. Nearshore chl-a was approximately twice offshore values, but the two series tracked each other closely over time, and the weak apparent increase in nearshore relative to offshore chl-a was driven primarily by the first four to five years of the series. Chl-a was therefore judged to reflect Gulf-wide oceanographic dynamics rather than localized nutrient pollution, and anthropogenic nitrogen inputs were adopted as the measure of eutrophication pressure.

The earlier implementation of the EUT component used municipal total nitrogen (TN) discharge estimates from Romero-Gil et al. (2026) as a single snapshot in time. Municipal TN was divided by coastline length and scaled against the maximum observed value, and municipality scores were averaged by coastline length within each region. That implementation had four limitations: (1) municipal reporting does not follow the way water reaches the Gulf, so loads could not be routed through the watershed pour points used for the other land-based CW pressures; (2) the source study did not cover Nayarit and Jalisco municipalities that fall within Region 9, so the Southeastern Gulf had to be gap-filled with the value for the Sinaloa Coast; (3) standardizing municipal loads by coastline length inflated the pressure attributed to Mexicali, the sole municipality in Region 1, which has intense livestock production relative to a short coastline, whereas hydrology-based routing was expected to place larger loads on the Sinaloa coast; and (4) the snapshot provided no temporal variation, so scores were carried forward unchanged across years.

*Updated method.* The EUT component was rebuilt by re-implementing the nitrogen-discharge methods of Romero-Gil et al. (2026) at the watershed scale, with watershed-to-pour-point-to-region assignment replacing municipal coastline standardization. Total nitrogen for each watershed $w$ and year $t$ is the sum of four sources, each expressed in tonnes of nitrogen per year:

$$
\text{TN}_{w,t} = N^{\text{ww}}_{w,t} + N^{\text{ag}}_{w,t} + N^{\text{liv}}_{w,t} + N^{\text{shrimp}}_{w,t}
$$

For each source, the coefficient from the supplementary sensitivity table of Romero-Gil et al. (2026) that was judged most appropriate for scoring was used.

**Wastewater.** Nitrogen from human wastewater was estimated as

$$
N^{\text{ww}} = \text{pop} \times \text{protein}_{\text{g/day}} \times 365 \times 0.16 \times (1 - \text{NRE})
$$

where pop is population, protein is per-capita protein consumption by age and sex (the mean consumption scenario), 0.16 is the nitrogen fraction of protein, and NRE is the nitrogen removal efficiency of wastewater treatment. Population was taken from the 2020 INEGI locality census (ITER), with localities of 2,500 or more inhabitants treated as urban and smaller localities as rural. Urban NRE was derived from CONAGUA wastewater treatment plant records, with removal efficiency weighted by flow and treatment process; rural areas were assigned NRE = 0, so that all nitrogen was assumed to reach water. Because plant flow values reported for 2020 contained apparent outliers, flagged values were set to missing and interpolated before NRE was computed. The 2020 baseline was scaled to other years using CONAPO municipal total-population ratios, and municipal loads were allocated to watersheds using 2020 locality-to-watershed shares.

**Agriculture.** Nitrogen from agriculture was estimated as the sum over crops $c$ of cultivated area multiplied by the fertilizer application rate and a leaching coefficient:

$$
N^{\text{ag}} = \sum_{c} \text{area}_c \times \text{fertilizer}_c \times L_c, \qquad L_c = 0.10
$$

Irrigated sown area by crop was obtained from DGSIAP agricultural production records, and fertilizer rates (kg N per hectare) from the crop-specific rates compiled by Romero-Gil et al. (2026) for the crops that account for most irrigated area. A leaching coefficient of 10% was used; the supplementary table reports 5% and 20% as alternatives, and the main text of the source study uses 20%. Municipal totals were allocated to watersheds in proportion to the share of CONABIO land use and vegetation (USV) cropland within each watershed. Estimates were produced for 2019–2025.

**Livestock.** Nitrogen from livestock was estimated as the product of animal numbers, species-specific nitrogen emission factors, and an export coefficient:

$$
N^{\text{liv}} = \left(\sum_{s} \text{heads}_s \times EF_s\right) \times E_{\text{export}}, \qquad E_{\text{export}} = 0.40
$$

Emission factors were 21.9 (cattle), 6.3 (goats), 4.1 (sheep), 4.1 (swine), and 0.79 (poultry) kg N per head per year. Municipal numbers of animals slaughtered were obtained from SIAP. A dasymetric approach was used to allocate municipal nitrogen to watersheds, using FAO Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4) species-specific density rasters as a proxy for where animals were located within each municipality. An export coefficient of 40% was used from the supplementary sensitivity table (alternatives of 70% and 100%; the source study main text uses 100%).

**Shrimp aquaculture.** Nitrogen from shrimp farming was estimated as

$$
N^{\text{shrimp}} = P_{\text{shrimp}} \times 47\ \text{kg N t}^{-1} \times E_{\text{export}}, \qquad E_{\text{export}} = 1.0
$$

Production by watershed was estimated from aquaculture land-use polygons by multiplying pond area by 1.5 t per hectare (González-Rivas et al. 2023), and the factor of 47 kg N per tonne of shrimp produced was adopted from Páez-Osuna (2007) as applied by Romero-Gil et al. (2026). Because shrimp ponds on the Gulf coast discharge effluents directly to adjacent estuarine or marine waters, 100% of the nitrogen was assumed to reach the sea, which represents an upper-bound scenario.

**Aggregation and routing.** Source tables were combined by watershed and year. Missing source years were gap-filled by watershed: observed years were retained as anchors, values were linearly interpolated between them (for example, for livestock in 2023 and for shrimp between land-use survey years), and the last observed value was carried forward to 2025 (for example, for shrimp after the 2021 survey). Only years in which all four sources were present were retained, yielding a multi-year series (`r eut_years_txt`; `r eut_n_years` years of scores). Watershed TN was then assigned to OHI regions through the watershed pour points (Figure 1) and summed within each region. Pour points are used only as a delivery and region-assignment step; no additional attenuation is applied between the pour point and the coast.

**Standardization and scoring (ALT method).** Regional TN was standardized by the length of mainland coastline within each region. Coastline was derived from the Natural Earth 1:10 m coastline clipped to the Gulf of California, with island coastlines removed by erasing a 1,500 m buffer around the Islas del Golfo de California protected-area polygon, and intersected with the OHI regions:

$$
TN_{\text{km}} = \frac{TN_{\text{region}}}{L_{\text{coast, km}}}
$$

The reference point was defined as the mean of the five highest TN per kilometer of coastline values across all regions and years ($TN_{\text{top5}}$), with an ideal of zero. The raw pressure is the proportion of this reference reached, capped at 1:

$$
\text{pressure}_{\text{raw}} = \min\left(1,\ \frac{TN_{\text{km}} - TN_{\text{ideal}}}{TN_{\text{top5}} - TN_{\text{ideal}}}\right), \qquad TN_{\text{ideal}} = 0
$$

In the alternative (ALT) scoring adopted for the updated method, the top-five-mean reference corresponds to a pressure of 0.5 rather than 1, so that

$$
\text{pressure} = 0.5 \times \text{pressure}_{\text{raw}}
$$

$$
\text{EUT status} = (1 - \text{pressure}) \times 100 = 50 + 50 \times (1 - \text{pressure}_{\text{raw}})
$$

Status therefore ranges from 50 to 100. A region with no TN receives a status of 100, a region at or above the top-five-mean reference receives a status of 50, and a region halfway to the reference receives a status of 75. This rescaling was adopted in preference to the scoring in which the reference maps to a status of 0, because the reference is an empirical benchmark derived from the highest loads observed within the Gulf rather than a threshold of complete impairment. Zero anthropogenic TN, the Mexican legal permissible TN limit in marine waters, and a global minimum TN value were also considered as references but were not adopted because of data limitations and the difficulty of converting annual loads into concentrations in a coastal setting where mixing is not a simple bathtub process. The updated method includes Region 9 directly, so no gap-filling from the Sinaloa Coast is required.

## Pathogens (PAT)

The Pathogens component was assessed using *Enterococcus* spp. as a fecal indicator bacterium, measured as the most probable number (*Número Más Probable*, NMP) per 100 mL from the CONAGUA *Playas Limpias* monitoring program at highly visited beaches of the Gulf of California for 2018–2025. Current monitoring (2022–2025) was combined with historical tables (2018, 2019, and 2021) digitized manually from the program website. No sampling was available for 2020 (COVID-19 pause), and that year was left missing rather than gap-filled.

Reference points followed the Mexican beach suitability standard, which classifies beaches as suitable (*Apta*) at 0–200 NMP/100 mL and unsuitable (*No Apta*) above 200 NMP/100 mL. The ideal was therefore 0 NMP/100 mL and the maximum was 200 NMP/100 mL. The upper threshold of 104 NMP/100 mL used by the California Blue Water Task Force for high *Enterococcus* levels was evaluated as an alternative but not retained, to apply Mexican rather than United States regulations. Sampling-site coordinates were converted from degrees–minutes–seconds to decimal degrees and intersected with the marine regions plus a 10 km inland buffer to assign each site to a region.

The program organizes data across three nested spatial levels below the OHI region: the sampling site (*sitio de muestreo*), the beach (*playa*), which may contain one or more sampling sites, and the coastal tourism destination (*destino*), which may contain one or more beaches (Figure 2).

![Figure 2. Visual depiction of the sitio → playa → destino hierarchy within *Enterococcus* spp. sampling and seasonal monitoring for the Playas Limpias Program.](figs/pathogen_sitio_playa_destino.png){width=90%}

Measurements were aggregated upward in a fixed order. First, NMP values were averaged (arithmetic mean) within site, season, and year. Second, sites were averaged within each beach, and third, beaches within each destination, for each season and year. Fourth, a status score was calculated for each destination, season, and year:

$$
\text{seasonal status} = \left(1 - \frac{\text{current NMP} - \text{ideal}}{\text{maximum} - \text{ideal}}\right) \times 100
$$

Fifth, the seasonal scores for each destination and year were combined using a geometric mean, so that a single poorly performing season meaningfully lowered the annual score:

$$
\text{annual destination score} = (\text{winter} \times \text{spring} \times \text{summer})^{1/3}
$$

If any season has a status of 0, the annual destination score becomes 0. Sixth, destinations were combined within each OHI region using a coastline-length weighted average, with weights derived from the Natural Earth 10 m coastline by buffering each sampling site by 1 km, intersecting the buffers with the coastline, and measuring the coastline sampled per destination and year (Mexico ITRF2008 / LCC). NMP values were aggregated with arithmetic means before any status transformation so that the status score reflected a single representative concentration for each destination and season, and the transformation did not interact with spatial averaging.

For gap-filling, the dataset was expanded to all region–year combinations from 2018 to 2025 and missing values were filled where appropriate, except for 2020. Monitoring in Region 3 (Mulegé) begins in 2023, so earlier values for that region should be treated as estimates rather than direct samples. Weighted and unweighted regional scores were compared across all years: in most regions the two differed by 0.0 to at most 2.1 points. The exception was Region 7 in 2025, where the weighted mean (48.6) diverged from the unweighted mean (61.3) because Guaymas, which had a long sampled coastline and an extreme exceedance in winter 2025 (destination mean of approximately 608 NMP/100 mL), received a large weight. The weighted mean was retained for all regions and years because it better reflects the spatial extent of contamination.

## Chemicals (CHM)

Chemicals are not a single pathway: agriculture, aquaculture, wastewater, contaminated sites, and vessels contribute through different routes. Five subcomponents were developed and combined with equal weights. Some region–year combinations have little or no applicable data for a subcomponent (for example, pesticides and hazardous waste in Region 1 and untreated wastewater in Region 2) and were treated as 100 in the combined Chemicals score.

**Pesticides.** Potential pesticide pressure was estimated from CONABIO land use and vegetation (USV) shapefiles for seven survey years (1985, 2001, 2005, 2009, 2013, 2016, and 2021) and national pesticide application rates (kg per hectare) for Mexico from FAOSTAT, available through 2023. Active cropland classes (rainfed, irrigated, moisture or floodplain, and occasional irrigated agriculture across annual, semi-permanent, and permanent subtypes) were retained, whereas secondary vegetation on former cropland and mixed agriculture–grassland and shifting-agriculture classes were excluded. Cropland was clipped to the coastal states using full state boundaries so that watersheds extending inland were fully captured, intersected with watersheds, and measured in hectares. Pesticide load by watershed and year was estimated as agricultural area multiplied by the national application rate (applied uniformly because sub-national and crop-specific rates were unavailable), summarized by watershed, and assigned to regions through pour points. Because the most recent USV survey was 2021, agricultural area was held constant at 2021 values for subsequent years, with the corresponding FAOSTAT rate applied for each scenario year. Status was calculated as

$$
\text{Pesticides score} = \left(1 - \frac{\text{current load} - \text{ideal}}{\text{maximum} - \text{ideal}}\right) \times 100
$$

with ideal = 0 kg and maximum = the mean of the five highest pesticide loads (kg per km of coastline) across regions and years.

**Pharmaceuticals.** Pharmaceutical contamination risk was estimated as the mass of pharmaceutical compounds (mg) potentially entering the Gulf from human wastewater, livestock antimicrobials, and shrimp-farming antimicrobials, aggregated by region and year and standardized by coastline length.

For human wastewater, CONAGUA SINA wastewater treatment plant operational data (2017–2023) for the six Gulf coastal states were intersected with watersheds. Annual effluent volume per plant was estimated by multiplying reported flow (L/s) by 31,536,000 seconds per year, which assumes continuous operation and is therefore an upper bound. Effluent was summed by watershed, joined to pour points within the 50 km inland buffer (with a 10 km buffer excluding Pacific-side pour points on the peninsula), and aggregated by region. Effluent volume was converted to pharmaceutical mass using mean concentrations from the literature (Vázquez-Tapia et al. 2020, supplemented with values from Garduño-Jiménez et al. 2023), restricted to contaminants of environmental concern (17β-estradiol, acetaminophen, caffeine, carbamazepine, diclofenac, ibuprofen, and naproxen; Hernández-Tenorio et al. 2024). Anomalous 2020 flow records affecting 258 plants in Regions 8 and 9 (a ratio to the plant median of more than 3 or less than 0.33, or a changed treatment process) were set to missing and linearly interpolated within each region.

For livestock, a dasymetric approach distributed municipal slaughter volumes (SIAP, 2006–2024) across 1 km cells using species-specific FAO GLW4 density rasters, with values multiplied by 101 mg of antimicrobial per kg (the North American use-intensity value of Acosta et al. 2025). Values were summarized by watershed and region, and 2023 values were interpolated because public SIAP data were missing. A sharp 2024 decline in cattle slaughter in Regions 1 and 2, present in the raw SIAP data and isolated to Baja California, was interpreted as a plausible real-world change and retained.

For shrimp farming, aquaculture polygons from the INEGI USV surveys (2005–2021) were intersected with watersheds, converted to production at 1.5 t per hectare (González-Rivas et al. 2023), and multiplied by 20.64 mg per kg (the North and Central America aquaculture antimicrobial use value of WOAH 2025).

Because these estimates represent different stages of use and release, multipliers were applied to estimate the fraction reaching the Gulf. For livestock, an excretion fraction of 60% (the midpoint of the 30–90% range in OECD guidance) and a runoff and leaching fraction of 5% (the conservative upper bound of published estimates of 0.2% to under 5%) were applied. For shrimp, a release fraction of 75% was applied to account for metabolic degradation, given that oral bioavailability of oxytetracycline in *Penaeus vannamei* of 43.6–48.2% (Uno et al. 2010) implies that nearly all applied compound reaches water through direct release or excretion, whereas other studies indicate that roughly 40–90% of applied antibiotics are released to the sea bottom. A multiplier of 1.0 was applied to wastewater, assuming that effluent residues reach coastal waters without additional attenuation.

Total mass was divided by mainland coastline length (Natural Earth 1:10 m coastline clipped to the Gulf, with island coastlines removed using a 1,500 m buffer). Status was calculated with the same formula as for pesticides, with ideal = 0 and maximum = the mean of the five highest mg-per-km values across regions and years; regions above the maximum were capped at a score of 0.

**Hazardous waste sites.** Hazardous waste status was assessed from the density and remediation status of sites in SEMARNAT and ASEA inventories located within the 50 km inland buffer of each region. Cumulative site density (cumulative number of identified sites per unit area) was rescaled with ideal = 0 sites and maximum = the mean of the five highest cumulative densities across regions and years, because even a remediated site is no longer pristine. A second score represented remediation progress, with each site assigned a value of 1 if remediated, 0.5 if it had an approved remediation plan or was being remediated, and 0 if no plan existed; the cumulative average across all sites in a region was used so that contaminated sites continued to contribute until remediated. The two scores were averaged:

$$
\text{Hazardous waste score} = \frac{\text{site density score} + \text{remediation score}}{2}
$$

**Untreated wastewater discharge points.** The density of municipal untreated wastewater discharge points was calculated from INEGI's National Census of Municipal Governments (CNGMD; 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023). Only discharge points with receptors that can carry untreated wastewater to the coast (beach, ocean, estuary or marsh, river or stream, canal or drain, and ground or ravine) were retained. Because points are reported by municipality, they were attributed to the corresponding municipality and region, and density was calculated as points per km² of region area. Status was calculated as for pesticides, with ideal = 0 points per km² and maximum = the highest observed density across regions and years.

**Vessel hydrocarbons.** Direct measurements of hydrocarbon releases were not available, so fishing vessel effort (hours of activity) was used as a proxy for the relative likelihood of chronic vessel-related pollution, including fuel and waste-oil discharge and accidental spills. No weighting by vessel size or type was applied. Mean vessel effort was calculated within each region for 2007–2025, and status was calculated as

$$
\text{Vessel hydrocarbons score} = \left(1 - \frac{\text{current effort} - \text{ideal}}{\text{maximum} - \text{ideal}}\right) \times 100
$$

with ideal = 0 and maximum = the mean of the five highest effort values across regions and years.

**Microplastics (explored, not scored).** Microplastics were explored as a particulate contaminant under Chemicals, using the NOAA NCEI global marine microplastics database (1972–2018) and Gulf-specific sediment data from Alvarez-Zeferino et al. (2020). The data were judged insufficient to calculate status scores: sediment samples were collected at only 0.05 m depth, which likely underestimates burial loads; some sites coincided with Hurricane Bud; conversion to particles per kg required assumptions about sand density; the most spatially comprehensive data represented a single year (2018); and nearshore and urban areas, where concentrations are likely highest, were poorly sampled. Surface-water concentrations from neuston and grab samples (Law et al. 2014; Barrows et al. 2018) were low and patchy and ended in 2018. Reviews of microplastic research in Mexico (Caro-Martínez et al. 2025; Vázquez-Morillas et al. 2024) report inconsistent protocols, varied units, and no national monitoring database. Microplastics were therefore excluded from the Chemicals mean.

## Marine Debris (MAR)

The Marine Debris component is intended to capture the prevalence of debris in the coastal waters of the Gulf. Plastics are a large share of beach litter in Mexico (SEMARNAT 2023), and large debris affects recreation, wildlife through entanglement and ingestion, and coastal aesthetics before breaking down into smaller particles. Several candidate large-plastics data sources were reviewed, including the SEMARNAT national plastics inventory and plastic-residue identification catalog, shrimp aquaculture best-practice guidance, CNGMD urban solid waste data (collection, treatment, and final disposal), beach cleanup tallies, citizen-science litter surveys, and remote sensing of very large floating objects. These describe the plastics problem and the land-based management context, but none provides a standardized, repeated measurement of trash on beaches or in nearshore waters by OHI region and year; CNGMD in particular measures waste-management systems on land rather than debris already present on the coast, and is closer to a pressure source or resilience layer. Plastic pollution is therefore treated descriptively, and Marine Debris status is calculated from ghost gear risk alone.

*Ghost gear risk.* Abandoned, lost, and discarded fishing gear (ALDFG) is a stressor of coastal and marine ecosystems (Gilman et al. 2021). It can kill marine mammals, sea turtles, and sharks, damage habitats, and create safety risks at sea. Ghost gear risk was estimated from vessel monitoring system (VMS) data for Mexican fishing vessels larger than 10.5 m with engines above 80 hp, which are required to carry transponders, paired with gear-specific abandonment, loss, and discard risk from Gilman et al. (2021, Table 2). Pings at speeds above 6 knots were excluded to retain active fishing positions, and the time contribution of each ping was capped at 3 hours. Each ping's contribution was calculated as

$$
\text{ghost gear risk}_{\text{ping}} = \text{Leakage risk}_{\text{gear}} \times \text{fishing hours}_{\text{ping}}
$$

For each year from 2007 to 2025, risk values were summed into 1 km grid cells, and the average risk was calculated for each OHI marine region. Pressure was rescaled to a 0–1 range using the mean of the five highest regional means across all regions and years as the maximum, with values capped at 1:

$$
\text{pressure} = \frac{\text{current ghost gear risk} - \text{ideal}}{\text{maximum} - \text{ideal}}, \qquad \text{Marine Debris score} = (1 - \text{pressure}) \times 100
$$

where ideal = 0.

# Results

## Overall Clean Waters status

Across the nine Gulf of California regions, CW current status varies in space and through time (Figure 3). Under the updated eutrophication method, the Gulf-wide mean of regional CW scores was approximately `r fmt1(s_cw$last)` out of 100 in `r s_cw$yr` (compared with `r fmt1(s_cw$first)` in `r s_cw$first_yr`; Figure 4). Regional scores in `r s_cw$yr` ranged from `r fmt1(s_cw$lo)` in the `r s_cw$lo_lab` to `r fmt1(s_cw$hi)` in the `r s_cw$hi_lab` (Figure 5). Higher CW scores indicate that a region is closer to unpolluted coastal waters across the pathways measured, whereas lower scores indicate that one or more pathways show elevated contamination. Because the overall score averages four pathways, the component and subcomponent results below should be examined to identify which pathway drives each regional result.

Components do not all cover the same years. Eutrophication spans `r eut_years_txt` under the updated method, Pathogens spans 2018–2025 with 2020 missing, and Chemicals and Marine Debris have longer series. Overall CW scores for years in which a component is missing are the mean of the available components, and gap-filled values for chemical pathways with no applicable data (treated as 100) can raise scores in places where the absence of data should not be read as pristine conditions. Overall CW values were `r if (cw_source_note == "precomputed") "read from the precomputed CW status table that incorporates the updated eutrophication scores" else "recalculated as the arithmetic mean of EUT, PAT, CHM, and MAR using the updated eutrophication scores"`.

Regional Clean Waters (CW) current-status scores (0–100) for nine OHI Gulf of California regions, calculated as the arithmetic mean of Eutrophication, Pathogens, Chemicals, and Marine Debris using the updated eutrophication method. The dashed line marks the reference condition (100)."}

## Eutrophication

Under the updated watershed-based nitrogen method, EUT is now a multi-year series covering `r eut_years_txt` (Figure 6) rather than a single snapshot carried forward. By construction, scores are bounded between 50 and 100, with 50 corresponding to a TN load per kilometer of coastline at or above the mean of the five highest values observed in the assessment. In `r s_eut$yr`, the Gulf-wide mean EUT score was approximately `r fmt1(s_eut$last)` (compared with `r fmt1(s_eut$first)` in `r s_eut$first_yr`; Figure 7), and regional scores ranged from `r fmt1(s_eut$lo)` in the `r s_eut$lo_lab` to `r fmt1(s_eut$hi)` in the `r s_eut$hi_lab` (Figure 8). Because the y-axes in Figures 6 and 7 begin at 40 to display the 50–100 range, differences among regions are visually emphasized relative to the other component figures, which use a 0–105 axis.

The routing of nitrogen through watershed pour points, the inclusion of Region 9 as a directly estimated region, and the use of multiple years of source data change the spatial pattern of eutrophication pressure relative to the earlier municipal snapshot, in which regional scores were determined by coastline-weighted municipal loads and Region 9 was assigned the Region 8 value. Temporal variation in the updated series reflects year-to-year change in the four sources, including population-scaled wastewater, agricultural area and fertilizer inputs, livestock slaughter, and shrimp-pond area, together with the interpolation and carry-forward rules described in the Methods.

## Pathogens

Pathogen status reflects *Enterococcus* concentrations at monitored beaches relative to the Mexican suitability threshold of 200 NMP/100 mL. The Gulf-wide mean Pathogens score in `r s_pat$yr` was approximately `r fmt1(s_pat$last)` (compared with `r fmt1(s_pat$first)` in `r s_pat$first_yr`; Figures 9 and 10), and regional scores in `r s_pat$yr` ranged from `r fmt1(s_pat$lo)` in the `r s_pat$lo_lab` to `r fmt1(s_pat$hi)` in the `r s_pat$hi_lab` (Figure 11). The 2025 value for Region 7 illustrates the influence of coastline weighting, because a single extreme exceedance at Guaymas in winter 2025 lowered the regional score substantially.

## Marine Debris

Marine Debris status is currently calculated from ghost gear risk alone. The Gulf-wide mean score in `r s_mar$yr` was approximately `r fmt1(s_mar$last)` (compared with `r fmt1(s_mar$first)` in `r s_mar$first_yr`; Figures 29 and 30), and regional scores ranged from `r fmt1(s_mar$lo)` in the `r s_mar$lo_lab` to `r fmt1(s_mar$hi)` in the `r s_mar$hi_lab` (Figure 31). Regional series can show abrupt changes in years when ghost gear risk in a region reaches the ceiling of the reference point; ghost gear risk in the Sinaloa Coast (Region 8) in 2017 is the clearest example and is interpreted as a reference-point scaling effect rather than a Gulf-wide change in debris.

# Discussion

This regional CW assessment demonstrates that clean coastal waters in the Gulf of California can be scored as the joint outcome of several contamination pathways that differ in origin, data availability, and spatial scale. Combining eutrophication, pathogens, chemicals, and marine debris in a single goal forces attention to the tradeoffs that single-pathway metrics obscure: a region may score well on directly monitored beach pathogens while carrying a high land-based chemical or nutrient burden, or the reverse. The component structure therefore functions as a diagnostic, in which the overall score identifies where clean-waters condition is lower and the components and subcomponents identify why.

**Updated eutrophication method.** The most consequential update in this assessment is the change in how eutrophication is estimated. The earlier approach relied on a single snapshot of municipal nitrogen discharge, which could not represent change through time, treated municipalities as the unit of analysis, omitted the Nayarit and Jalisco municipalities in Region 9, and, by dividing by coastline length, attributed disproportionate pressure to a municipality (Mexicali) with a short coast and intensive livestock production. The updated method addresses each of these issues. By estimating nitrogen by watershed and assigning it to regions through the same pour points used for the pesticide and pharmaceutical indicators, EUT now follows the hydrological logic used throughout the Chemicals component and allows source categories to be combined consistently across indicators. Using wastewater, agricultural, livestock, and shrimp aquaculture sources with annual inputs through 2025 produces a time series that can respond to changes in population, cropland, animal numbers, and pond area, and that can be updated as new source data become available. The inclusion of Region 9 removes the need to substitute another region's value.

The ALT scoring also changes the interpretation of the score. Setting the pressure associated with the mean of the five highest TN loads per kilometer of coast to 0.5 produces a status range of 50 to 100, so that even the most heavily loaded regions do not score 0 solely because they define the empirical benchmark. This choice reflects the fact that the reference is a relative, within-Gulf benchmark rather than an ecological or legal threshold, but it has consequences that should be recognized. The compressed range reduces the influence of EUT on the overall CW score relative to a 0–100 scale, and the status of a region cannot be read as the distance to a toxicological or regulatory limit. Several alternative references remain under consideration, including Mexican legal permissible TN concentrations, which could not be applied because converting annual loads to concentrations requires assumptions about coastal water volume and mixing that would overstate confidence.

Several uncertainties remain in the nitrogen estimates. Wastewater loads rely on 2020 census population scaled with municipal projections and on treatment-plant flows that contain apparent reporting anomalies; agricultural loads use a 10% leaching coefficient and crop-specific fertilizer rates; livestock loads use a 40% export coefficient and an allocation of municipal values by modeled animal density; and shrimp loads assume that all nitrogen reaches the sea. Alternative coefficients from the source study are available and could be used to evaluate sensitivity of regional ranks. Gap-filling by interpolation and carry-forward, particularly for shrimp after the 2021 land-use survey and livestock in 2023, means that the most recent years of the series are partly projected rather than observed.

**Pathogens as the monitored component.** Pathogens is the only component anchored to an explicit regulatory threshold and a direct measurement, which makes it the most readily interpretable but also the most sensitive to monitoring design. The 2020 gap, the late start of monitoring in Region 3, and the dependence of regional scores on which beaches are sampled and how they are weighted by coastline length all affect comparability across regions and years. The use of a geometric mean across seasons deliberately penalizes destinations with at least one poor season, and the coastline-weighted regional mean better reflects spatial extent of contamination, as shown by the Region 7 2025 result.

**Chemicals as an integrated land-based pressure.** The Chemicals component integrates five pathways at the cost of using different data types: modeled loads (pesticides and pharmaceuticals), inventories (hazardous waste), municipal census counts (untreated wastewater), and an effort-based proxy (vessels). Equal weights are applied because no basis exists for ranking the consequences of the pathways, and alternatives such as consequence-based weights or a geometric mean across subcomponents were considered but not adopted. Treating no-data region–year combinations as 100 prevents spurious penalties but can inflate scores where data are absent, and this should be considered when interpreting regions with fewer applicable data. Microplastics, which could help describe particulate contamination, were not scored because available data are insufficient in spatial coverage, temporal extent, and methodological consistency.

**Marine debris and unscored pathways.** Basing Marine Debris on ghost gear alone is a pragmatic choice that omits visible large plastics and beach litter, which are among the most noticeable forms of marine pollution to coastal residents and visitors. Data on solid waste management, beach cleanups, and remote sensing describe land-based management or are too uneven to support a Gulf-wide, multi-year regional status layer, and they are best treated as context or resilience information until standardized, repeated monitoring exists. Other pathways were raised during development but are not currently scored, including sedimentation, noise and light pollution, harmful algal blooms, water clarity, and dissolved oxygen; they either lack consistent data or their link to anthropogenic eutrophication is unclear in the Gulf.

**Goal-level aggregation and limitations.** An arithmetic mean was chosen for the overall goal because a geometric mean allowed a reference-point artifact (ghost gear in Region 8 in 2017) to drive the whole score toward zero. This choice is more tolerant of a single poor pathway, and future work should evaluate weighted alternatives and test whether pathways such as pathogens and chemicals warrant greater weight. Reference points that rely on the highest observed Gulf pressures, as in the pesticide, pharmaceutical, hazardous waste, vessel, ghost gear, and eutrophication indicators, produce relative rankings and could in future be replaced with absolute ecological or legal thresholds where they exist. Subjective decisions of this kind are central to any health index and should be explicitly aligned with regional values (Halpern et al. 2014).

Despite these constraints, the CW framework provides a transparent, repeatable scorecard for clean coastal waters in the Gulf of California. The updated eutrophication method, in particular, aligns nutrient pressure with the hydrological and temporal structure of the other land-based indicators and offers a foundation for future updates as new data become available.

# Data and code availability {.unnumbered}

Current-status outputs and intermediate tables are stored under the OHI Gulf of California goal-preparation directories for Clean Waters (`goal_prep/cw/v2025/`). Updated eutrophication scores are produced by the watershed-based nitrogen workflow in `eutrophication/jarg_analysis_update/` (source scripts for wastewater, agriculture, livestock, shrimp aquaculture, total nitrogen, and the ALT status calculation) and written to `nutrient_status_ALT.csv`. The overall CW table incorporating the updated eutrophication scores is `cw_current_status_arithmetic_w_updated_EUTR.csv`, in which the Marine Debris component is labeled PLA. Processing scripts for pathogens, chemicals, and marine debris are maintained in the project Clean Waters workflow. Interactive visualization of related scores is available via the OHI Gulf of California project website.
